turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hey, Mr. Ellison, come on in and have a seat. What got you in today?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, it's this cough, doctor. Dry, tickly, right in the throat, and I kept telling myself it was just a cold, but it's been hanging on and my wife basically pushed me out the door.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did the cough actually start?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I almost said two weeks, but that's wrong. The cold was three weeks ago, and the dry cough started with it, so three weeks. I lose track because the days all feel the same when you're hacking.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the cold itself, is any of that still going?

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Runny nose, scratchy throat, that stuff lasted a few days and then it quit. Nose is fine now, throat doesn't hurt. The cough is the only thing that stuck around, which is why I blamed the cold and waited.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is it there all day, or more at certain times?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): All day, but nights are worse, right in the throat. Lying down sets it off, and if I talk a lot, like I'm doing right now, it bubbles up. Sipping water calms the tickle for a minute and then it's back. I moved to the guest room so my wife can sleep, which she appreciates and also does not.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever with this? Shortness of breath?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. I checked with the old thermometer twice and I wasn't hot. I'm not short of breath either. I walk the dog around the block every morning and I can do that fine, it's just embarrassing when I cough the whole way.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain at all? Any wheezing?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. And I don't wheeze, it's not that tight whistling thing, it's just a dry hack. I started to go off on a whole story about the dog and, um, I'll spare you.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you coughing anything up, mucus or blood?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing at all. Dry as a bone. I tried honey in tea because my neighbor, not a doctor, swears by it, and it tasted fine and did basically nothing. Sorry, that's a tangent.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): No problem. You're followed for blood pressure. Tell me what you're actually taking these days.

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): High blood pressure for, um, five-ish years, maybe a bit more, I never remember the exact anniversary. The water pill is hydrochlorothiazide. I always want to say twelve and a half milligrams, but I looked, it's twenty-five milligrams, once every morning, and I've been on that one for years.

[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): And then two weeks ago we added ramipril. I had it in my head that it was twenty milligrams, but the bottle this morning says ten milligrams, once a day. Both of them by mouth, with breakfast, every day. I don't skip.

[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me say that back. Hydrochlorothiazide twenty-five milligrams each morning for years, ramipril ten milligrams each morning for the last two weeks, both by mouth. That's the list?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the whole list. No vitamins, no aspirin, I know everybody my age is on aspirin but I'm not. And I blamed the cold for the cough, not the new pill.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): What made you think it wasn't the ramipril?

[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): My brother Dave has high blood pressure too, and he's on lisinopril, I think twenty milligrams, and he has never coughed from it. So I figured if he can take an ACE inhibitor, mine shouldn't be the problem. His pill, not mine, I just mean the comparison.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Got it, his lisinopril stays his. We'll come back to the timing. Any medicine allergies, or food, anything like that?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. Penicillin is fine, aspirin is fine, I've never swollen up or gotten a rash from a drug. I feel like I should have a more interesting answer and I don't.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): So no known allergies. Do you smoke?

[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Never have. My dad did and the house smelled like an ashtray, so I never started. I'll have a beer on Sundays watching the game, that's the alcohol story, very boring. I still work part-time at the hardware store, mostly the garden section.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any surgeries in the past?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Appendix out when I was twenty-two. Emergency, middle of the night, very dramatic at the time and completely irrelevant now. Nothing since.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. I'm going to check your pressure and listen to your chest. Give me a second.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Sure. The cuff always squeezes more than I expect. I tell myself that every visit and it still surprises me.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-six. Heart rate seventy-four. Oxygen sat ninety-eight percent.

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Office number looks decent. At home it's been up in the one-fifties, which is the whole reason we added the ramipril. I keep a notebook, very analog, my wife wants me to use an app.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lungs are clear, I don't hear any wheeze, your throat looks normal, and there's no swelling in the legs.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, good. I was half convinced you'd find something rattling around in there. The cough feels so loud from the inside.

[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me pull the story together before I say what I think. Dry cough for three weeks, started with a cold, runny nose and scratchy throat gone after a few days, worse at night and lying down, water helps only briefly.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. And no fever, no phlegm, no chest pain, I can breathe fine.

[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the medicines: water pill twenty-five milligrams for years, ramipril ten milligrams started two weeks ago, so the cough actually began about a week before the ramipril.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Huh. I hadn't lined it up like that. I was so stuck on the cold idea that I didn't count the days against the pill. That's a little annoying, that I missed it.

[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to call this a definite drug cough. It could be the ramipril, those can cause a dry cough in some people, and it could also just be the tail of the cold, since it started first and your exam is clear.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): So you're saying it might be either, and you don't know yet.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's exactly it. I can't say for sure today which one it is. What I do want to do is stop the ramipril and switch you to losartan, fifty milligrams once a day.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Losartan. Is that still for the blood pressure? And fifty milligrams, not twenty-five? I mix numbers up, I want to hear it twice.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, for the blood pressure. Fifty milligrams, once each morning, by mouth. Keep the hydrochlorothiazide at twenty-five. Don't take any more ramipril, starting now.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Stop ramipril today, start losartan tomorrow morning with the water pill. I won't borrow my brother's lisinopril, that was never the plan, I was only talking.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. If your lips or tongue swell, or your chest gets tight, that needs the emergency room, don't wait for me.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Lips, tongue, tight chest, ER. Got it. What about the cough itself, do I take something for it, like a suppressant from the pharmacy?
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't add a cough syrup right now. Let's see what happens off the ramipril. Honey and water are fine if they soothe you, just don't expect them to fix it.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Fair. And if it doesn't settle, or if it gets worse before I see you?

[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it gets worse, or you get breathless, a fever, or chest pain, call us or go to urgent care, don't sit on it. Otherwise I want you back here in four weeks to recheck the pressure and see about the cough.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks either way, even if the cough vanishes next Tuesday.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Even if it vanishes. The four-week visit is for the blood pressure on losartan, not only the cough.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. I over-explain, I know. The hardware store thing, the dog, the notebook, none of that changes the pill. I just don't like leaving stuff out.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): The timeline was the useful part. Anything else you wanted to ask while you're here?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Um. Will the losartan make me dizzy? The ramipril didn't, but new pills make me nervous. Also the pharmacy by the grocery closes at six and I parked in the short lot.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can make some people lightheaded, especially the first few doses. Stand up slowly, and if you feel faint, sit down and call us. Most people do fine.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Stand up slow, call if faint. I can do that. I'll start it tomorrow, not tonight, like you said.
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tomorrow morning is right. I'll see you in four weeks, Mr. Ellison.

spec.situation: Hypertension patient with a dry cough for weeks that they connect to 'a cold'; recently started ramipril or enalapril; they mention a relative's lisinopril. Doctor thinks aloud, changes the drug but does not give a firm diagnosis of the cough.
features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

omissions.text: Ramipril 10 mg and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg are both taken by mouth each morning with breakfast, and the patient reports he does not skip doses.
The patient is not taking vitamins or aspirin.
No known drug allergies were clarified with examples: penicillin is fine, aspirin is fine, and he has never had swelling or a rash from a drug.
Home blood pressures have been in the 150s, which was the reason ramipril was added.
Dry cough causes sleep disruption/significant nighttime impact: he moved to the guest room because nights are worse and lying down triggers it.
The doctor advised the 4-week follow-up is for blood pressure reassessment on losartan even if the cough resolves sooner.
Possible losartan adverse effect counseling: it can cause lightheadedness, especially with the first few doses.
